title: Finding Exoplanets
objective: After this level you can explain the transit and wobble methods for finding planets around other stars.
summary: Since 1995, astronomers have found more than 6,000 exoplanets, mostly from the dips and wobbles they cause in their stars.

cards.headline: Thousands of planets found, and almost none of them actually seen.
Worlds beyond the Sun
cards.body: An exoplanet is a planet orbiting a star other than the Sun. In 1995 Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz found the first around a Sun-like star, 51 Pegasi b, work that earned the 2019 Nobel Prize in Physics. Today more than 6,000 are confirmed.
cards.callout: 1995: the first around a Sun-like star

cards.headline: Dips and wobbles
cards.body: Most exoplanets are found indirectly. The transit method watches for the small, regular dip in a star’s light when a planet passes in front of it. The wobble method detects the slight back-and-forth motion a planet’s gravity gives its star, measured through shifts in the star’s spectrum.

cards.fact: NASA’s Kepler telescope found thousands of exoplanets.
cards.context: It stared at the same patch of sky for years, watching for tiny dips in starlight as planets crossed their stars.

questions.explanation: An exoplanet is any planet orbiting a star other than the Sun.

questions.prompt: How does the transit method detect a planet?

options.label: By a small, regular dip in the star’s light
By hearing the planet’s radio signals
By measuring the star’s color change

questions.explanation: When a planet passes in front of its star, the star’s light dips slightly, again and again on each orbit.

questions.prompt: From Level 32: how do spectra help find planets with the wobble method?

options.label: They show the planet’s own colors
options.rationale: The planet’s light is swamped by the star’s.

options.label: The star’s spectral lines shift as it wobbles

questions.explanation: As the planet tugs its star back and forth, the star’s spectral lines shift slightly, revealing the unseen planet.
